transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Acme Head of ML), Ethan Chu (Acme Infra), Priya Nair (Acme Research)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive on quantization strategies (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ), accuracy regressions, runtime impacts (latency/throughput), KV cache and batching interactions, and on-prem/VPC deployment considerations. Action items and next steps agreed.

[00:00] Jamie: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to spend most of this hour on the quantization review and how it impacts your latency and accuracy targets. may I do a quick roll call?
[00:07] Maya: maya here, hi
[00:09] Ethan: ethan here
[00:10] Priya: priya here
[00:12] Ravi: ravi from redwood se
[00:15] Jamie: cool ok so agenda: quick lit of approaches (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, awq), tradeoffs, runtime implications, then we'll go into benchmarks and your constraints, and decide pilot next steps. sound good?
[00:25] Maya: yep

[02:10] Ravi: so starting high-level - INT8 is the most mature quant path in our runtime: stable kernels, predictable latency and memory reduction ~2-4x depending on model and activations. but accuracy can slip on some layers; we usually do per-channel scaling and asymmetric quant to reduce loss.
[02:45] Ethan: sorry quick Q, when you say kernels are mature, do you mean GPU kernels or CPU fallback? our pilot is on A100s and some T4s for staging.
[02:54] Ravi: mostly GPU kernels; INT8 on A100 has good support with cuBLAS/CUTLASS-esque paths. t4 is okay but you see less perf win. CPU INT8 will help for embedding workloads but less so for decoder LM heavy inference.

[05:20] Priya: what about FP8? there's talk of FP8 on hopper/h100 series, we might spin up H100s later. how does it compare?
[05:28] Ravi: FP8 (the newer e4m3/e5m2 variants) gives FP-like dynamic range, so smaller accuracy regressions vs INT8 in many cases. the caveat: hardware support matters. on H100/Hopper you get native FP8 with very good throughput; however the toolchain and kernel stability are less mature than INT8 for general models. also quantization-aware calibration for FP8 is different - you often need activation-sensitive calibration or mixed precision layers.

[07:15] Maya: and GPTQ / AWQ? we've seen papers claiming near-lossless 4-bit quant with GPTQ; AWQ is newer, says it preserves accuracy with asymmetric weight quantization. how do they behave in our runtime?
[07:30] Ravi: GPTQ is weight-only post-training quantization that uses second-order info to minimize layer-wise error; it can do 4-bit and often 3-4 bit with small deltas on perplexity for many models. main tradeoffs: GPTQ artifacts are model-specific and can be fragile across prompt distributions. runtime-wise, GPTQ-quantized models generally need custom kernels (int4 paths) and those can be high-throughput but less flexible for KV cache fusion unless we add special handling.
[08:10] Ravi: AWQ is more recent and tries to do per-group asymmetric quant which often gives better accuracy at same bitrate versus naive int4; we have an experimental AWQ path in our internal builds. it looks promising but we recommend running evals per-customer.

[09:45] Ethan: you mentioned KV cache - does quantization change KV cache size or correctness?
[09:52] Ravi: good question. two parts: (1) memory: quantizing weights reduces model footprint, but KV cache size depends on activations (hidden states) which are typically float16/float32 unless you quantize activations which is uncommon for autoregressive LMs. so KV cache RAM for sequence length stays similar unless you change activation dtype. (2) correctness: some int4/GPTQ kernels require dequantize/compute/requantize steps that complicate streaming KV cache updates; we've seen increased latency tails because of those conversions if kernels are not fused carefully. for production SLOs we recommend measuring tail latency with realistic streaming loads.

[12:05] Priya: how about batching and throughput? we assume quantized models improve throughput, but does small batching to meet latency SLOs reduce the win?
[12:15] Ravi: exactly - batching multiplies arithmetic throughput; quantized models increase matrix multiply throughput per GPU, but if your latency SLO demands small batch sizes (1-4) then you might not saturate the GPU and you'll see diminished speedups. in our tests, for 13B with int8, peak throughput can be 2.5-3x vs fp16 with large batch; but at batch=1 the latency win is ~20-40% depending on kernel fusion and NVLink config.

[14:00] Maya: any recommendations for hybrid strategies? we have a 99th pct latency target of 250ms for small queries and throughput requirement for daytime spikes.
[14:12] Ravi: yes hybrid routing: route latency-sensitive traffic to FP16 or FP8 variants with smaller batch or dedicated nodes; route background/bulk requests to INT8/GPTQ nodes. Redwood's smart routing can do that by policy (latency vs cost). also automatic fallback to a less-quantized variant when regressions are detected.

[16:40] Ethan: hardware question: for on-prem/VPC we might have a mixed fleet with some H100 and some A100s. how do quantization choices change?
[16:50] Ravi: if you have H100s, FP8 is attractive because of native support and throughput; on A100, FP8 is not hardware-native so you'd rely on emulation which is slower. INT8/GPTQ works on both but kernel performance differs. we recommend pinning model variants per host type and using our serving runtime to route accordingly.

[19:30] Priya: accuracy regressions - what magnitude should we expect? and how to measure acceptance?
[19:36] Ravi: depends on model and task. for instruction-tuned 7B models: INT8 might give <1-3% drop on classifier-style metrics, GPTQ 4-bit often <2-5% on many language metrics but can have outliers. AWQ often reduces outliers. we suggest a small eval suite: 50-200 prompts across your critical flows, measure task-specific metrics (exact-match/F1 or human eval) and define delta thresholds (e.g., <=2% absolute drop or human acceptability).

[22:12] Maya: we care about hallucination rate and instruction-following. are there known failure modes from GPTQ/AWQ?
[22:20] Ravi: yes some failure modes: scaling collapse in early layers causing verbatim repetition, or numeric saturation leading to token misranking. in instruction-following you may see subtle style drift. that's why we recommend layered QA: (1) automatic evals, (2) spot human review of top-failure prompts, (3) rollout with canary traffic.

[25:05] Jamie: practical: our runtime supports per-route model variants and canary rollouts. we can also keep a small percent of requests on fp16 for diff checks to detect regressions in live traffic.

[26:30] Ethan: is there any impact to observability / tracing when using custom kernels like GPTQ?
[26:37] Ravi: observability remains: we get token-level latency, cost accounting etc. but detailed granular layer-level traces depend on kernel integration. some experimental int4 kernels don't have fine-grained timing for each matmuls, so we put coarse timings and microbenchmarks to flag performance regressions.

[28:10] Priya: calibration steps - do we need per-customer calibration data?
[28:17] Ravi: best practice is to calibrate on representative data. for INT8 we do calibration to get activation ranges; for AWQ/GPTQ you often run a small calibration/eval corpus to select per-layer parameters. we can either run in our sandbox (you provide prompts) or we can provide a tooling container for you to run on-prem so data never leaves your VPC.

[31:00] Maya: what about legal/compliance concerns with on-prem quant builds and KMS?
[31:07] Jamie: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs; for on-prem we can package the quantized model artifacts and the runtime container; no code leaves your environment if you prefer. we also support SOC2 controls and SSO/SAML for console access.

[33:00] Ravi: quick note on kernel selection: runtime picks optimized kernels by model size, sequence length distribution, and hardware. for GPTQ/AWQ we add specialized int4 kernels and a dequant path. those kernels are heavily optimized but we still recommend per-workload microbenching to tune block sizes and group sizes.

[35:45] Ethan: any known compatibility issues with KV cache persistence when we do checkpointing and warm restart?
[35:53] Ravi: checkpointing is fine as long as the runtime serializes the activation dtype correctly. problem arises if you mix variants (e.g., warm start from fp16 to int4) - that's unsupported. maintain same model variant for restore. we can help with migration patterns.

[38:10] Priya: can you share an example metric table from your previous pilots? like latency/throughput and accuracy delta?
[38:20] Ravi: yes i'll share an anonymized spreadsheet - typical row: model (7B/13B), dtype (fp16/int8/awq/gptq), batch sizes, avg latency (ms), p95 latency (ms), tokens/sec, accuracy delta (%). 7B int8 peak tokens/sec ~2.8x fp16 on A100, but p95 latency at batch=1 only ~30-35% lower. gptq 4-bit tokens/sec close to int8 in many cases but with more variance.

[42:00] Maya: question on rollout: we want to start with an internal pilot for docs summarization tasks. what would you recommend as pilot scope?
[42:10] Jamie: pilot scope suggestion: pick 7B model, run 4 variants (fp16 baseline, int8 static, gptq 4-bit, awq 4-bit), run 50-100 prompts representative of summarization + 20 edge cases for hallucination. measure n-rouge/ROUGE-L, hallucination rate, human rating, latency p50/p95. if AWQ/GPTQ meet accuracy thresholds, then expand to 13B.

[45:30] Ethan: networking: for private deployment we have multi-tenant VPC subnets and strict egress. anything special to configure for hardware kernels?
[45:40] Jamie: nothing special kernel-wise, but for on-prem packaging we provide docker images and helm charts. if you have H100s behind private AMI drivers, we'll need node labels so runtime schedules proper kernels to H100 nodes. also ensure image pull secrets and KMS configs are set.

[47:00] Priya: any tips to reduce accuracy regressions other than trying different quant schemes? like fine-tuning after quant?
[47:10] Ravi: quant-aware fine-tuning helps a lot: a few thousand steps of QAT or low-rate fine-tune on your instruction dataset can recover many losses. alternatively, you can keep sensitive heads/layers in fp16 (mixed quant) — i.e., hybrid quantization. AWQ often implicitly keeps some granularity, but mixed precision is a solid fallback.

[50:15] Maya: curious: how do you detect regressions early in production?
[50:22] Ravi: we run live diff sampling: send a small % of traffic to baseline fp16 and quantized variant, compute automated ranking diffs and a small human-in-the-loop panel for flagged failures. Redwood Optimize can alert on drift beyond thresholds.

[52:40] Jamie: ok let's recap action items and next steps
[52:45] Maya: yes please
[52:47] Jamie: recap: ravi will run AWQ vs GPTQ vs INT8 benchmarks on your 7B/13B models with your 50 prompts, produce spreadsheet; maya will share prompts and failure cases; jamie will send quantization whitepaper and packaging notes for on-prem and KMS; we'll schedule follow-up week of 2025-03-24 to review results and plan pilot.
[53:20] Priya: sounds good
[53:25] Ethan: thanks all
[53:28] Ravi: one more note: when we run benchmarks we'll include tail latency under streaming scenarios and a batch scenario, that way you can see both latency-sensitive and throughput wins.
[54:00] Jamie: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the links and the spreadsheet.
[54:10] Maya: thanks
[54:12] Priya: bye

End of transcript
